title: Patient Survey Translation and Complaint Language Access
summary: Translate patient surveys and support complaints across languages while preserving question meaning, privacy, response options, and follow-up.
body_markdown:
###


Survey translation converts written questions, response options, instructions, and reminders into another language, while complaint interpretation supports a live spoken exchange. A U.S. healthcare feedback program may need both, and it should keep the source text, translated text, interpretation method, and follow-up record distinct.


###


A hospital should use only survey languages, modes, and administration procedures authorized by the current HCAHPS program for official submission. Locally translated questions can support local improvement work, but the hospital should keep them separate from standardized reporting unless the program’s current rules permit their use.


###


The team should preserve the concept, reference period, response scale, skip instructions, and neutral tone, then test the translation with speakers of the intended language. For U.S. patient-experience work, version each approved translation and document cognitive interviews or other testing so score changes are not confused with wording changes.


###


The organization should provide language support for complaint intake, acknowledgments, clarification requests, status updates, resolution, and applicable appeal information. Confirm the patient’s preferred spoken and written languages, route urgent safety concerns outside routine survey queues, and document who owns the response.


###


Leaders should measure eligible patients, invitations sent, successful delivery, completion, unanswered items, complaint acknowledgment, resolution time, and unresolved communication needs by language when privacy permits. Report denominators and suppress small groups that could identify individuals instead of treating missing feedback as a positive care result.
